newsitem.title: JAPAN: JSDA says does not plan to restrict new OTC shares.
newsitem.headline: JSDA says does not plan to restrict new OTC shares.

text.p: The Japan Securities Dealers Association (JSDA) does not plan to restrict the registration of new over-the-counter shares, Tsugio Yukihira, acting chairman of the JSDA, said on Wednesday.
He also told reporters that a scandal involving Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Japan's top securities house, had not undermined overall business in Japan's securities market.
Yukihira said that the over-the-counter market had been deteriorating because of declining participation by individual investors and net selling from investment trusts and others.

To cope with the worsening supply and demand situation in the OTC market, JSDA has been considering the introduction of an OTC margin trading system and a new registration system using the book-building method.
Japan's Finance Ministry is also considering introducing a market-maker system in order to ensure liquidity in the OTC market.

Another JSDA official said, however, that securities houses which help companies register new shares on the OTC market and issuers themselves may suspend new share registrations because of the current poor market situation.
Yukihira said that he did not see any signs that trading volumes on Japan's stock markets or that the underwriting of corporate bonds had declined due to the Nomura scandal.
Nomura is currently under investigation by Japanese regulators due to suspected illegal deals by two former senior executives involving a "sokaiya" racketeer.

Yukihira said that Japanese securities houses will face tough business conditions as a result of the nation's "Big Bang" financial reforms, which are expected to include an end to fixed stock broking commissions.
"The securities industry as a whole must focus on streamlining and restructuring to cope with the expected difficulties," he said.
He also said that the Ministry of Finance (MOF) would not oppose any voluntary moves by unprofitable brokers to shut down their operations.
Japan's securities houses operate under licences granted by MOF.
No Japanese securities house has closed down and given back its licence to the ministry since the system began in the 1960s, industry sources said.

"There must be a way for businesses to close down voluntarily without causing trouble for their customers. If such trouble was taken care of, the finance ministry would not oppose voluntarily closure," Yukihira said.
